claim: Caulobacter crescentus is a synchronizable model bacterium.
source: In this study, we show that the capsule of the synchronizable model bacterium Caulobacter crescentus is cell cycle regulated
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established characteristic of the organism.

claim: The capsule of Caulobacter crescentus is cell cycle regulated.
source: In this study, we show that the capsule of the synchronizable model bacterium Caulobacter crescentus is cell cycle regulated
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: HvyA is a bacterial transglutaminase homolog that prevents capsulation in G1-phase cells.
source: we unearth a bacterial transglutaminase homolog, HvyA, as restriction factor that prevents capsulation in G1-phase cells
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by genetic and biochemical data in the results.

claim: The capsule protects Caulobacter cells from infection by bacteriophage φCr30.
source: This capsule protects cells from infection by a generalized transducing Caulobacter phage (φCr30)
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phage sensitivity assays and Tn-Seq data in the results.

claim: Loss of HvyA confers insensitivity to bacteriophage φCr30.
source: the loss of HvyA confers insensitivity towards φCr30
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by phage spot tests showing ΔhvyA cells are resistant to φCr30.

claim: The multi-layered regulatory circuitry directing HvyA expression to G1-phase is conserved during evolution.
source: Moreover, the multi-layered regulatory circuitry directing HvyA expression to G1-phase is conserved during evolution
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing MucR regulation of hvyA orthologs in Sinorhizobia.

claim: HvyA orthologues from related Sinorhizobia can prevent capsulation in Caulobacter.
source: HvyA orthologues from related Sinorhizobia can prevent capsulation in Caulobacter
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by complementation experiments showing SMc00998 and NGR_c12490 restore φCr30 sensitivity.

claim: Alpha-proteobacteria have retained HvyA activity.
source: indicating that alpha-proteobacteria have retained HvyA activity
evidence: This is inferred from the functional complementation data with heterologous HvyA orthologs.

claim: Genetic exchange is fundamental to bacterial adaptation to changing environmental conditions.
source: Genetic exchange is both fundamental to the adaptation of bacterial cells faced with ever-changing environmental conditions and the cause of the alarming dissemination of antibiotic resistance determinants among the bacterial pathogens.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Genetic exchange is the cause of dissemination of antibiotic resistance determinants among bacterial pathogens.
source: Genetic exchange is both fundamental to the adaptation of bacterial cells faced with ever-changing environmental conditions and the cause of the alarming dissemination of antibiotic resistance determinants among the bacterial pathogens.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Mechanisms of genetic exchange include transformation, conjugation, and generalized transduction.
source: The underlying mechanisms include direct uptake of naked DNA (transformation) by bacterial cells as well as cell- or bacteriophage-based delivery systems (respectively conjugation and generalized transduction) (Wiedenbeck and Cohan, 2011; Seitz and Blokesch, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Components of the pneumococcal natural transformation machinery can be linked to cell division spatially.
source: Recent cytological experiments provide evidence that components of the pneumococcal natural transformation (competence) machinery can be linked to cell division, at least spatially (Bergé et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated as prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Microbial polysaccharidic capsules can restrict bacteriophage-mediated genetic exchange.
source: Microbial polysaccharidic capsules can also restrict bacteriophage-mediated genetic exchange.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Capsules mask bacteriophage receptor sites on or near the cell surface.
source: Typically, they mask bacteriophage receptor sites that are on or near the cell surface (Hyman and Abedon, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Capsules are virulence factors in many Gram-negative and Gram-positive species.
source: Moreover, capsules are virulence factors in many Gram-negative and Gram-positive species, as they provide immune evasion by shielding or camouflaging the targets of host immune cells that are located on the surface of bacterial cells (Schneider et al., 2007; Kadioglu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Capsulation can be regulated by nutritional cues.
source: While capsulation can be regulated by nutritional cues (Kadioglu et al., 2008; Yother, 2011), cell envelope stresses (Laubacher and Ades, 2008) or physical cues (Sledjeski and Gottesman, 1996; Tschowri et al., 2009; Loh et al., 2013), no systemic cues are currently known.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Capsulation can be regulated by cell envelope stresses.
source: While capsulation can be regulated by nutritional cues (Kadioglu et al., 2008; Yother, 2011), cell envelope stresses (Laubacher and Ades, 2008) or physical cues (Sledjeski and Gottesman, 1996; Tschowri et al., 2009; Loh et al., 2013), no systemic cues are currently known.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Capsulation can be regulated by physical cues.
source: While capsulation can be regulated by nutritional cues (Kadioglu et al., 2008; Yother, 2011), cell envelope stresses (Laubacher and Ades, 2008) or physical cues (Sledjeski and Gottesman, 1996; Tschowri et al., 2009; Loh et al., 2013), no systemic cues are currently known.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: No systemic cues regulating capsulation are currently known.
source: While capsulation can be regulated by nutritional cues (Kadioglu et al., 2008; Yother, 2011), cell envelope stresses (Laubacher and Ades, 2008) or physical cues (Sledjeski and Gottesman, 1996; Tschowri et al., 2009; Loh et al., 2013), no systemic cues are currently known.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus is capsulated.
source: The synchronizable and capsulated alpha-proteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus (henceforth Caulobacter) is the pre-eminent model system for cell cycle studies (Ravenscroft et al., 1991; Skerker and Laub, 2004; Curtis and Brun, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic supported by citations.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus is the pre-eminent model system for cell cycle studies.
source: The synchronizable and capsulated alpha-proteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus (henceforth Caulobacter) is the pre-eminent model system for cell cycle studies (Ravenscroft et al., 1991; Skerker and Laub, 2004; Curtis and Brun, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Asymmetric cell division in Caulobacter yields a motile and piliated swarmer cell in G1-arrested state and a sessile stalked cell in S-phase.
source: In Caulobacter this asymmetric cell division yields a motile and piliated swarmer (SW) cell that is in a G1-arrested state and a sessile stalked (ST) cell that resides in S-phase (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The cellular buoyancy of stalked cells is higher than that of swarmer cells.
source: The cellular buoyancy of the latter is higher than the former, a feature that has been exploited for synchronization of Caulobacter populations (by density gradient centrifugation) (Ely, 1991) for cell cycle studies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Density gradient centrifugation has been exploited for synchronization of Caulobacter populations.
source: The cellular buoyancy of the latter is higher than the former, a feature that has been exploited for synchronization of Caulobacter populations (by density gradient centrifugation) (Ely, 1991) for cell cycle studies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A vast number of transcripts are cell cycle-regulated in Caulobacter.
source: A vast number of transcripts are cell cycle-regulated in Caulobacter (Laub et al., 2000) and in the alpha-proteobacterium Sinorhizobium meliloti (De Nisco et al., 2014), a plant symbiont.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A vast number of transcripts are cell cycle-regulated in Sinorhizobium meliloti.
source: A vast number of transcripts are cell cycle-regulated in Caulobacter (Laub et al., 2000) and in the alpha-proteobacterium Sinorhizobium meliloti (De Nisco et al., 2014), a plant symbiont.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CtrA is a conserved and essential cell cycle transcriptional regulator.
source: Importantly, many transcripts of orthologous genes are cell cycle-regulated and this is in large part governed by the conserved and essential cell cycle transcriptional regulator A (CtrA).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: CtrA activates transcription of many late S- and G1-phase genes.
source: CtrA activates transcription of many late S- and G1-phase genes that are repressed by the transcriptional regulators SciP or the MucR1/2 paralogs, respectively (Fumeaux et al., 2014; Gora et al., 2010; Tan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SciP represses late S-phase genes activated by CtrA.
source: CtrA activates transcription of many late S- and G1-phase genes that are repressed by the transcriptional regulators SciP or the MucR1/2 paralogs, respectively (Fumeaux et al., 2014; Gora et al., 2010; Tan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MucR1/2 paralogs repress G1-phase genes activated by CtrA.
source: CtrA activates transcription of many late S- and G1-phase genes that are repressed by the transcriptional regulators SciP or the MucR1/2 paralogs, respectively (Fumeaux et al., 2014; Gora et al., 2010; Tan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CtrA functions as a negative regulator of DNA replication initiation by binding to the Caulobacter origin of replication.
source: In addition to acting as a transcriptional activator, CtrA functions as a negative regulator of gene expression and DNA replication initiation by binding to the conserved 5′-TTAA-(N)7-TTAA-3′ motif (CtrA box) located in many Caulobacter and Sinorhizobium promoters (Laub et al., 2000, 2002; Fumeaux et al., 2014) and the Caulobacter origin of replication (Cori) (Quon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CtrA binds to the conserved 5′-TTAA-(N)7-TTAA-3′ motif (CtrA box) in many Caulobacter and Sinorhizobium promoters.
source: In addition to acting as a transcriptional activator, CtrA functions as a negative regulator of gene expression and DNA replication initiation by binding to the conserved 5′-TTAA-(N)7-TTAA-3′ motif (CtrA box) located in many Caulobacter and Sinorhizobium promoters (Laub et al., 2000, 2002; Fumeaux et al., 2014) and the Caulobacter origin of replication (Cori) (Quon et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CtrA∼P is present in G1-phase, proteolyzed during the G1→S transition, and re-accumulates later in S-phase.
source: CtrA∼P is present in G1-phase, proteolyzed during the G1→S transition to permit replication initiation and re-accumulates later in S-phase (Domian et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: G1-phase transcription is positively dependent on PleC.
source: G1-phase transcription is also positively dependent on PleC (Wang et al., 1993), a phosphatase that is sequestered to the SW cell pole at cell division (Wheeler and Shapiro, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PleC is a phosphatase that is sequestered to the swarmer cell pole at cell division.
source: G1-phase transcription is also positively dependent on PleC (Wang et al., 1993), a phosphatase that is sequestered to the SW cell pole at cell division (Wheeler and Shapiro, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PleC regulates cellular buoyancy properties.
source: While PleC also regulates the cellular buoyancy properties, the molecular basis has never been determined.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a gap that this study addresses.

claim: HvyA is the first example of a factor restricting phage infection to a confined cell cycle phase.
source: As the capsule protects Caulobacter cells from infection by the generalized transducing Caulophage φCr30 and no CRISPR/Cas (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats–CRISPR associated)-based adaptive immunity system to protect cells from invading genetic material is encoded in the Caulobacter genome (Marks et al., 2010), HvyA is the first example of a factor restricting phage infection to a confined cell cycle phase.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the findings and the absence of CRISPR/Cas in Caulobacter.

claim: No CRISPR/Cas-based adaptive immunity system is encoded in the Caulobacter genome.
source: As the capsule protects Caulobacter cells from infection by the generalized transducing Caulophage φCr30 and no CRISPR/Cas (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats–CRISPR associated)-based adaptive immunity system to protect cells from invading genetic material is encoded in the Caulobacter genome (Marks et al., 2010), HvyA is the first example of a factor restricting phage infection to a confined cell cycle phase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Density gradient centrifugation of WT Caulobacter culture yields stalked and pre-divisional cells with high buoyancy ('light') and swarmer cells with low buoyancy ('heavy').
source: Density gradient centrifugation of a WT culture yields ST and PD cells with the characteristic high buoyancy (for simplicity, we refer to these cells as 'light') and SW cells with the characteristic low buoyancy ('heavy' cells, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: ΔpleC cells are exclusively 'light'.
source: As ΔpleC cells are exclusively 'light', we simply sought himar1 transposon (Tn) insertions that render ΔpleC cells 'heavy' (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Transposon insertions in ΔpleC cells that render them 'heavy' map to two loci.
source: After backcrossing such 'heavy' ΔpleC::Tn mutants, we mapped the Tn insertion sites to two loci (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The first locus identified encodes putative components of a group 1 (Wzy)-like capsular polysaccharide export machinery.
source: The first locus (Figure 1C, upper panel) encodes putative components of a group 1 (Wzy)-like capsular polysaccharide (CPS) export machinery, in which the saccharide precursors are first assembled on undecaprenol (Und∼P, black zigzag in Figure 1D) on the cytoplasmic membrane, flipped and assembled in the periplasm into a polymer that is then translocated across the outer membrane and anchored on the cell surface (Whitfield, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: Transposon insertions were found in genes encoding CCNA_00162, CCNA_00163, CCNA_00164, CCNA_00167, and CCNA_00168.
source: Tn insertions were found in the genes encoding a putative capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis lipoprotein (CCNA_00162), a Wzc-like chain length regulator/tyrosine kinase (CCNA_00163), a putative O-antigen polymerase/ligase (CCNA_00164), a putative Wzb-like metallophosphatase (CCNA_00167), and a Wza-like outer membrane translocon (CCNA_00168), all commonly associated with capsular export systems.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on transposon mutagenesis data.

claim: No transposon insertions were found in CCNA_00166 (hvyA) or pssY.
source: No Tn insertions were found in the other two genes within this cluster, CCNA_00166 and pssY.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on transposon mutagenesis data.

claim: CCNA_00166 is predicted to encode a putative bacterial transglutaminase-like cysteine protease (BTLCP).
source: By contrast, CCNA_00166 is predicted to encode a putative bacterial transglutaminase-like cysteine protease (BTLCP)
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis and prediction.

claim: An in-frame deletion of CCNA_00166 (ΔhvyA) in WT cells resulted in 'light' cells.
source: we describe below that an in-frame deletion of CCNA_00166 (ΔhvyA in Figure 1C) in WT cells resulted in 'light' cells, akin to ΔpleC cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Deleting pssY did not render cells 'heavy'.
source: Consistent with the results from the Tn analysis, an in-frame deletion (Figure 1C) in pssY did not render cells 'heavy'.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on genetic deletion experiments.

claim: Deleting CCNA_00162, CCNA_00163, CCNA_00164, or CCNA_00167 gave rise to 'heavy' WT and ΔpleC cells.
source: By contrast, deleting CCNA_00162, CCNA_00163, CCNA_00164, or ΔCCNA_00167 gave rise to 'heavy' WT (and ΔpleC) cells (Figure 1C and Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: Complementation of deletion mutants with plasmid-borne genes restored the WT buoyancy phenotype.
source: Moreover, complementation of ΔCCNA_00162, ΔCCNA_00163, ΔCCNA_00164, ΔCCNA_00167, or CCNA_00168::Tn mutant cells with a plasmid harbouring the corresponding gene under the control of the vanillate inducible promoter (Pvan) on a medium–copy number plasmid (pMT335 (Thanbichler et al., 2007)) restored the WT buoyancy phenotype, showing that the 'heavy' phenotype is attributable to the loss of CCNA_00162, CCNA_00163, CCNA_00164, CCNA_00167, or CCNA_00168 function (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on complementation experiments.

claim: The second cluster of genes resides on a 26-kbp mobile genetic element (MGE).
source: The second cluster of genes resides on a 26-kbp mobile genetic element (MGE) that has previously been implicated in buoyancy (Marks et al., 2010) (Figure 1C, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results supported by a citation and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Transposon insertions were recovered in CCNA_03998, CCNA_00470, and CCNA_00471.
source: Specifically, we recovered Tn insertions in genes predicted to encode a homolog of the putative N-acetyl-L-fucosamine transferase WbuB from E. coli that is involved in O-antigen (O26) synthesis (D'Souza et al., 2002) (CCNA_03998), a polysaccharide polymerase (CCNA_00470) and a GDP-L-fucose synthase (CCNA_00471).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on transposon mutagenesis data.

claim: In-frame deletions in CCNA_03998 or CCNA_00470 in WT or ΔpleC cells resulted in 'heavy' cells.
source: To confirm that CCNA_03998, CCNA_00470, and CCNA_00471 are indeed buoyancy determinants, we engineered in-frame deletions in CCNA_03998 or CCNA_00470 (CCNA_00471 was not tested) in WT or ΔpleC mutant cells and found the resulting single or double mutants to be 'heavy' (Figures 1C and 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: All 'heavy' mutants exhibited a non-mucoid ('rough') colony phenotype on PYE agar plates supplemented with 3% sucrose.
source: Indeed, all 'heavy' mutants exhibited a non-mucoid ('rough') colony phenotype on PYE agar plates supplemented with 3% sucrose, while the WT or 'light' mutants (ΔpleC) had a mucoid ('smooth') colony appearance (Figure 2A,B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: WT and 'light' mutants (ΔpleC) had a mucoid ('smooth') colony appearance on PYE agar plates supplemented with 3% sucrose.
source: Indeed, all 'heavy' mutants exhibited a non-mucoid ('rough') colony phenotype on PYE agar plates supplemented with 3% sucrose, while the WT or 'light' mutants (ΔpleC) had a mucoid ('smooth') colony appearance (Figure 2A,B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The Caulobacter capsule is primarily composed of neutral monosaccharides including fucose, mannose, galactose, and glucose.
source: As the Caulobacter capsule is primarily composed of neutral monosaccharides including fucose, mannose, galactose, and glucose (Ravenscroft et al., 1991), we used glycosyl compositional analysis as proxy to quantify capsular material from 'heavy' and 'light' strains (See 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Fucose, galactose, and mannose were abundant in capsule preparations from WT and ΔhvyA cells.
source: As shown in Table 1, the expected sugars (determined as % of total carbohydrate weight in the preparations) were abundant in preparations from the WT and the 'light' mutant (ΔhvyA, Table 1)
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: Capsule preparations from 'heavy' mutants (ΔCCNA_00163 and ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00163) contained far less fucose, galactose, and mannose compared to 'light' mutants.
source: whereas those from the 'heavy' mutants (i.e. the ΔCCNA_00163 single mutant and the ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00163 double mutant) contained far less fucose, galactose, and mannose (up to 37-fold, 23-fold, and 5.5-fold reductions, respectively, in the ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00163 double mutant compared to the ΔhvyA single mutant).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: A significant reduction in galacturonic acid was observed in preparations from 'heavy' mutants vs WT or 'light' cells.
source: We also observed a significant reduction in galacturonic acid in the preparations from the 'heavy' mutants vs WT or 'light' cells, raising the possibility that this saccharide is also a constituent of the NA1000 capsule (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: The loss of capsule synthesis and/or export renders cells 'heavy' and 'rough'.
source: Taken together, our results show that the loss of capsule synthesis and/or export renders cells 'heavy' and 'rough' and that the loss of capsulation is epistatic to the loss of PleC in buoyancy control.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: The loss of capsulation is epistatic to the loss of PleC in buoyancy control.
source: Taken together, our results show that the loss of capsule synthesis and/or export renders cells 'heavy' and 'rough' and that the loss of capsulation is epistatic to the loss of PleC in buoyancy control.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: PleC, directly or indirectly, regulates one of the newly identified buoyancy determinants.
source: On these grounds we predicted that PleC, directly or indirectly, regulates one of the newly identified buoyancy determinants.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the results based on the epistasis data.

claim: PleC is required to turn off capsule synthesis in G1-phase swarmer cells.
source: Since the buoyancy switch is cell cycle-regulated and since all ΔpleC cells are 'light' (Figure 1B), we reasoned that PleC is required to turn off capsule synthesis in G1-phase SW cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the buoyancy data.

claim: Division of ΔpleC yields two daughter cells that are capsulated, non-piliated and non-motile.
source: As PleC is also required to activate motility and PilA (the structural subunit of the pilus filament) expression, when ΔpleC divides two daughter cells that are capsulated, non-piliated and non-motile are formed.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on known functions of PleC and the buoyancy data.

claim: Division of WT Caulobacter yields one piliated, motile, and non-capsulated ('heavy') G1-phase swarmer progeny and one capsulated ('light') S-phase stalked cell.
source: By contrast division of WT yields one piliated, motile, and non-capsulated ('heavy') G1-phase SW progeny and one capsulated ('light') S-phase ST cell (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: PleC is required for the accumulation of the transcript of CCNA_00166 (hvyA).
source: Interestingly, PleC is required for the accumulation of the transcript of CCNA_00166 (referred to as hvyA due to its requirement to render cells 'heavy') (Chen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The hvyA transcript peaks during the G1-phase.
source: The hvyA transcript peaks during the G1-phase and encodes a 272-residue protein (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: HvyA encodes a 272-residue protein.
source: The hvyA transcript peaks during the G1-phase and encodes a 272-residue protein (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: HvyA harbours a classical N-terminal Sec-dependent signal sequence.
source: harbouring a classical N-terminal Sec-dependent signal sequence (SS), but lacking discernible hydrophobic sequences or a lipidation signal for retention in the membrane, suggesting that it is periplasmic.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence analysis.

claim: HvyA lacks discernible hydrophobic sequences or a lipidation signal for retention in the membrane.
source: harbouring a classical N-terminal Sec-dependent signal sequence (SS), but lacking discernible hydrophobic sequences or a lipidation signal for retention in the membrane, suggesting that it is periplasmic.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence analysis.

claim: HvyA is predicted to be periplasmic.
source: harbouring a classical N-terminal Sec-dependent signal sequence (SS), but lacking discernible hydrophobic sequences or a lipidation signal for retention in the membrane, suggesting that it is periplasmic.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on sequence analysis.

claim: The C-terminal part of HvyA features a BTLCP domain.
source: The C-terminal part of HvyA features a BTLCP domain.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence analysis.

claim: The BTLCP domain is thought to introduce intra- or inter-molecular crosslinks by transamidation.
source: This domain is thought to introduce intra- or inter-molecular crosslinks by transamidation, forming γ-glutamyl-ε-lysine isopeptide bonds between Gln and Lys residues, to hydrolyse amide bonds by the reverse protease reaction and/or to execute deamidation/esterification reactions of glutamine residues (Lorand and Graham, 2003; Ginalski et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cysteine proteases typically feature a Cys-His-Asp catalytic triad.
source: Cysteine proteases typically feature a Cys-His-Asp catalytic triad (C192, H226, and D241 for HvyA, based on sequence alignment, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and applied to HvyA based on sequence alignment.

claim: HvyA has a predicted catalytic triad consisting of C192, H226, and D241.
source: Cysteine proteases typically feature a Cys-His-Asp catalytic triad (C192, H226, and D241 for HvyA, based on sequence alignment, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ΔhvyA phenocopied the buoyancy defect of ΔpleC cells (yielding exclusively 'light' mucoid cells).
source: As an in-frame deletion in hvyA (ΔhvyA) phenocopied the buoyancy defect of ΔpleC cells (yielding exclusively 'light' mucoid cells, Figures 1b, 2a, 2b), we conclude that HvyA is required for capsule-mediated buoyancy control in Caulobacter.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figures 1B, 2A, and 2B.

claim: HvyA is required for capsule-mediated buoyancy control in Caulobacter.
source: As an in-frame deletion in hvyA (ΔhvyA) phenocopied the buoyancy defect of ΔpleC cells (yielding exclusively 'light' mucoid cells, Figures 1b, 2a, 2b), we conclude that HvyA is required for capsule-mediated buoyancy control in Caulobacter.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the genetic data.

claim: Expression of WT HvyA from Pvan reversed the buoyancy defect of ΔhvyA and ΔpleC cells.
source: While expression of WT HvyA from Pvan (pMT335-hvyA) reversed the buoyancy defect of ΔhvyA and ΔpleC cells, analogous plasmids encoding the predicted catalytic mutants (C192S/A, H226Q/A, or D241A) were unable to do so
evidence: This is stated in the results based on complementation experiments.

claim: Plasmids encoding the predicted catalytic mutants (C192S/A, H226Q/A, or D241A) were unable to reverse the buoyancy defect of ΔhvyA and ΔpleC cells.
source: While expression of WT HvyA from Pvan (pMT335-hvyA) reversed the buoyancy defect of ΔhvyA and ΔpleC cells, analogous plasmids encoding the predicted catalytic mutants (C192S/A, H226Q/A, or D241A) were unable to do so
evidence: This is stated in the results based on complementation experiments.

claim: All HvyA variants (WT and catalytic mutants) accumulated to comparable steady-state levels.
source: although all the HvyA variants accumulated to comparable steady-state levels as the WT protein on immunoblots (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of catalytically active HvyA is necessary and sufficient to mitigate the buoyancy defect of ΔpleC cells.
source: Thus expression of catalytically active HvyA is necessary and sufficient to mitigate the buoyancy defect of ΔpleC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the complementation data.

claim: Mutations in capsule synthesis and export genes are epistatic to both the ΔhvyA and ΔpleC mutations.
source: As a genetic selection for 'heavy' ΔhvyA::Tn mutants was answered by Tn insertions in the same genes that render ΔpleC cells 'heavy' (Figure 1C), we reasoned that mutations in capsule synthesis and export genes are epistatic to both the ΔhvyA and ΔpleC mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the genetic data.

claim: ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00163, ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00167, ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00470, and ΔpleC ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00167 mutants are 'heavy' and non-mucoid ('rough').
source: To confirm this notion, we engineered ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00163, ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00167, and ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00470 double mutants as well as a ΔpleC ΔhvyA ΔCCNA_00167 triple mutant and found all resulting mutants to be 'heavy' and non-mucoid ('rough') on PYE sucrose plates (Figure 2A, B and Supplementary File 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and 2B.
